newsitem.title: USA: Clinton health plan for children may fall short.
newsitem.headline: Clinton health plan for children may fall short.

text.p: President Clinton's proposal to expand health insurance to children is not likely to achieve his stated goal of reaching 5 million kids by the year 2000, health analysts and congressional sources said.

Analysts said the plan, unveiled last week as part of Clinton's balanced budget proposal, contains questionable assumptions while taking credit for insuring hundreds of thousands of children already due to receive coverage under current law.
"It doesn't do a lot," one health policy analyst said. "The president, in his State of the Union address, artfully said he would cover 'up to' five million children."

Analysts complained Clinton's budget does not include funding to carry out what administration officials have billed as an aggressive effort to enroll 1.6 million more poor children in the Medicaid programme by 2000.
They also said it was not clear governors would go along with voluntary efforts to expand care to millions of children at a time when Clinton wants to limit Medicaid spending.
An estimated 10 million U.S. children are uninsured.
A White House official defended the proposal, saying Clinton had made health insurance for children a top priority even as other programmes were being cut to balance the budget.

"The president got $18 billion in investments for health. If you use that well, you may get a significant number of kids covered," he said. "If people can find different ways, the president didn't say 'it's my way or no way.'"
Some provisions of the plan are winning support.

Letting states keep children in the Medicaid programme a full year at a time, rather than having periodically to recertify their eligibility, could keep children from falling off the rolls -- if governors agree to implement it. The White House said the change will aid 1 million children.

The plan's biggest chunk of money -- $9.8 billion over five years to pay insurance premiums for workers between jobs -- is also winning support. It would buy six-month insurance for 3.3 million people, including 700,000 children.

"Probably most concrete is what last year they called their initiative for the temporarily unemployed. It's being cast a little more as a children's piece," said Ron Pollack of Families USA, which lobbies for health care expansion.
Congressional Democrats, who labeled covering children up to age 18 as their top health priority, praise Clinton. But they, and some Republicans, will work around the White House.
"It doesnt extend far enough," Massachusetts Democrat Sen. John Kerry said.

Overall, the administration plan calls for $18.4 billion in spending over five years. It reaches most of the 5 million children by bringing them into Medicaid, which insures more than 37 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans.
Health Secretary Donna Shalala has promised renewed efforts to reach half of an estimated 3 million poor children who are eligible for Medicaid but not enrolled.
"It's going to take a large public-private partnership to find them," Shalala said. "Everyone has told me it's going to be very tough, but we're determined."
Clinton's budget does not include new money for outreach to find the 1.6 million kids. Officials say they will work through existing programmes such as Head Start and immunisation efforts.
Shalala plans also to work with managed care plans, which cover more than 12 million Medicaid recipients and have a financial interest in signing up unenrolled children.
State officials question the effort, saying many governors already have major outreach efforts.

"There are a range of issues that need to be explored before we start assuming that, at the drop of a hat, 2 million kids are going to come on to Medicaid," an official working with governors said. Others said outreach would be costly.

The administration also counts toward its 5 million total 1 million poor adolescents who will become eligible for Medicaid under current law, which gradually phases in benefits to poor children up to age 19.

The White House says 250,000 more children will receive Medicaid each year through 2000 under the phase-in. However, the Congressional Budget Office re-examined the law and believes only 125,000 children will become eligible annually.

The plan includes $750 million in annual grants for states to work with private groups to expand coverage, insuring 1 million children. Republicans question whether the funding, about $15 million a year per state, would reach that many. White House officials count the grants as indirect outreach that will pick up 400,000 Medicaid children.
